quote:
Growth and survival of vegetation in China's arid and semi-arid
regions are strongly limited by the availability of water (Donohue et al.,
2007). Due to the large amounts of soil moisture consumed by fast-
growing vegetation, a dry soil layer to a depth of 2 m or more often
develops when grassland and farmland are invaded by woody
vegetation and there is insufﬁcient precipitation to replace the water
consumed by this vegetation (Liu et al., 2004, 2008b). This dried soil
layer creates a formidable barrier between vegetation and the under-
ground water, and thereby limits vegetation establishment and
subsequent growth (Cong et al., 2010; Zhu and Meng, 2010). For
example, dwarf trees, which are locally called “old-man small-trees”,
have been observed throughout reforestation regions in the Loess
Plateau (McVicar et al., 2010). This metaphor vividly describes the low
growth rates and poor health of man-made forests when water levels
are inadequate, and forests of these trees cannot provide the desired
ecological functions of soil and water conservation and carbon
sequestration. The high mortality and sub-optimal growth rates of
these trees in the Loess Plateau have illustrated the difﬁculty of
afforestation in China's arid and semi-arid regions.
label: Soil-water mechanism
disposition: Water deficit limits establishment; drylayer2m describes consequence, not soil-depth minimum.

quote:
3. Synthesis and recommendations
Niche differentiation caused by differences in soil water availability
can directly determine both local- and regional-scale distributions of
species (Engelbrecht et al., 2007). Vegetation restoration solutions
must therefore be tailored to the water availability and other
ecological conditions in a region (Normile, 2007). When afforestation
is performed, it may initially increase forest cover, but its impact on
biodiversity and its ability to achieve ecological restoration will
depend on the type of reforestation carried out and its suitability for
the local environment (Lamb et al., 2005). In arid regions, a biological
and chemical crust usually forms in the surface layer of an undisturbed
soil, providing resistance to wind erosion and retarding evaporation
from the soil (Normile, 2007). If that crust is broken by plowing for
agriculture, by grazing livestock, or by planting of trees, the protection
of the soil is lost and, as a result, evaporation and erosion may increase,
leading to a loss of vegetation that may be difﬁcult to repair (Normile,
2007).
Most deliberate efforts to overcome such degradation of sites have
focused exclusively on tree planting, often with inappropriate species
selection or inappropriate early stand management, leading to
plantation failures (Lamb et al., 2005). In some cases, the vegetation
originally present at a site is removed during planting of the trees to
reduce competition between the planted trees and other plants (Cao
et al., 2009a). To conserve species richness and protect the native
species and the ecological services they provide, it may be more
efﬁcient to focus conservation funds on non-forest ecosystems and
low-carbon forests (Miles and Kapos, 2008). Some successful policies,
such as the prohibition of grazing and logging, encouraging decreases
in the area of cultivated land, and conservation of natural vegetation,
should be prioritized. Except to protect man-made landscapes (as in

disposition: Tailor to water availability; protect natural nonforest ecosystems. No global grassland exclusion inferred.

Table 1).
For example, the Natural Forest Conservation Program plans to reforest
4.4 million ha from 2000 to 2010 by means of planting and aerial
seeding (State Forestry Administration, 2009). Except for the Wildlife
Conservation and Nature Reserves Development Program, the focus of
the new policies is how to grow more forests and how to shift from
natural vegetation to man-made forests. As a result of these programs,
from 1952 to 2008 more than 27.2% of China's area was either artiﬁcially
planted (230 million ha) or seeded by air (30.7 million ha) (Fig. 2). The
area of afforestation has increased rapidly, and the State Forest
Administration claims that environmental degradation has begun to
reverse (Liu et al., 2008a). However, there is strong evidence that
contradicts these claims. First, the overall survival rate of trees in
afforestation projects from 1952 to 2005 has been only 24% (Wang et al.,
2007). Tree survival across the Three Norths Shelter Forest System
Project during this period was only 15% (Li, 2001; Cao, 2008a). Second,
serious water-related soil erosion has expanded during the past
30 years to cover an additional 1000 km2 of land annually (Wan et al.,
2005; Normile, 2007). Third, for arid and semi-arid China as a whole, the
desertiﬁcation rate (the proportion of China's total area that experi-
enced desertiﬁcation in a givenyear) increased by 11% in themid-1950s,
57% in the mid-1980s, and 19% in the early 2000s (Wang et al., 2010).
Monitoring data has demonstrated little relationship between the
afforestation projects and the frequency and intensity of dust storms in
northern China (Wang et al., 2010), and sandstorms continue to sweep
northern China and surrounding areas (Fig. 3). In contrast to some
ofﬁcial claims, these factors contribute to China's environmental
sustainability index remainingamongthe lowest in theworld (Stokstad,
2005; Liu and Diamond, 2008).

quote:
Another scheme based on planting of local tree and shrub species
has become popular in China recently. Unfortunately, the complex
combination of biophysical processes, biochemical cycles, and bio-
social relationships have limited this work. For example, Populus
tremula is sometimes found where precipitation is as low as 180 mm
per year, usually near rivers and other areas where water is more
abundant than in the surrounding area, but is more often found where
precipitation is nearer to 1000 mm (Cao, 2008b). Atlowerprecipitation
levels, this species must exploit deep soil water to survive, lowering the
water table and making it impossible for shallow-rooted vegetation to
survive; as a result, planting this species can lead to man-made
desertiﬁcation (Fig. S2). Salix psammophila is a familiar shrub in semi-
arid to humid parts of the Mu Us Sandland of northern Shaanxi Province.
label: Species examples
disposition: Populus precipitation180/near1000mm observations and Salix riverbank requirement are species-specific, not practice rules. Stop species-envelope extraction under user gate; retain pointer.
